questions.prompt: A festival's website prints one paragraph for each show. Match each part of this paragraph with the column of the programme table it fills.

options.text: the Northern Players, a young company from Bizerte
in the courtyard of the Bell Tower Playhouse
every evening from 3 to 21 July, Mondays excepted
The Storm Season, a comedy in three acts
Dates
Play
Troupe
Venue

questions.explanation: Reading a programme is squeezing prose into four fields, and each field takes one kind of thing. People who act together are a troupe, and the sentence that names them tells you nothing about where they will be. The place of the performance is the courtyard, given down to the building it belongs to — a reader who wrote down the town instead would still not know which door to walk through. A stretch of evenings with an exception inside it is a run, so it fills the column of dates, and the title with its subtitle is the work itself. Notice that the paragraph gives them in no particular order: it is the reader who sorts them.

questions.prompt: A pupil has written four lines of a report on a drama festival. In one of them he has used a word of this lesson for something the word does not name. Which line must he correct?

options.text: The troupe was built in 1927 and holds nine hundred.
The venue is an open-air theatre above the harbour.
The choreography was designed by a dancer from Cairo.
The playwright finished the text in under three weeks.

questions.explanation: A troupe is a group of human beings; nothing about it can be built in a given year or hold a given number of people. What the pupil has described is the place the performance happens in, and English has a word ready for it in the same lesson. The three other lines each put their word where it belongs: an open-air theatre is indeed the place of a performance, dance steps are indeed invented by a person, and the text of a play is indeed the work of the one who writes plays.

questions.prompt: Reading the programme you meet this line: "By eight o'clock the audience was heading for the ruins." You do not know the expression "heading for". Which word do you go looking for in your dictionary?

options.text: heading
was heading
head
for

questions.explanation: A dictionary files verbs under their base form, so an ending has to be stripped off before you start turning pages: what you are carrying to the shelf is head. The form with its ending will not be listed on its own, and neither will the whole verb group, which belongs to this sentence and to no other. The preposition does have an entry of its own, but it will tell you about direction in general and never about this expression — which you will find inside the entry for the verb, printed in the little example that shows exactly which preposition has to follow.

questions.prompt: Three notes stand under one heading in a pupil's file: "Work before the theatre: fisherman · sign-painter · night watchman". Which sentence turns the three of them into a single sentence of English?

options.text: Before he came to the theatre: fisherman, then sign-painter, then night watchman.
Before he came to the theatre he was a fisherman, and he hated every single day of it.
He was a fisherman. He was a sign-painter. He was a night watchman. Then the theatre.
Before he came to the theatre he was a fisherman, a sign-painter and a night watchman.

questions.explanation: Three notes under one heading are three items of one list, and English strings a list of three with commas and a final and, inside one sentence that carries one subject and one verb. Replacing the punctuation of the file with the word then keeps the note exactly as it was, verb and subject still missing. Three separate sentences with the same opening give the reader the same information three times over and read like a form being filled in. And what the man felt about the work is written nowhere in the file: a writer who supplies it has left the notes behind.

questions.prompt: A festival office writes to a newspaper: "Our Shakespeare week is now on the calendar for the first fortnight of April." What has the office just announced?

options.text: the week has been called off and will not happen
the week is planned, and its dates are now fixed
the week has been moved from April to the autumn
the week is still being discussed with the town

questions.explanation: Something that is on the calendar has a place of its own in the year's plan: it is decided, and the days it will occupy are known. That is precisely why a festival office sends the sentence to a newspaper — readers can now write the fortnight into their own year. An event still under discussion has no dates to give, and an event called off has left the calendar rather than joined it. As for the month, the sentence names April as the fortnight it holds, not as the month it is leaving.

questions.prompt: Before any of these lines can go into a biography, some of them have to be turned into full sentences. Tick EVERY line that is still written as a note.

options.text: 1943: first part in a school play
She played her first part in a school play at thirteen.
Married at twenty-two; two daughters
Left the company after a quarrel with its director
He left the company after a quarrel with its director.

questions.explanation: A note is recognised by what is missing from it. A year followed by a colon has no verb at all and no person to attach it to. A past participle standing alone with a semicolon after it has neither subject nor tense, and the two daughters arrive with no verb to bring them. The third one is subtler and worth studying beside its neighbour: the same words appear twice, once without a subject and once with one, and only the second is a sentence — the words alone were never the problem, the missing person was. The remaining line was complete from the start.
